newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Thais capture Khmer Rouge hardliner - Cambodian PM.
newsitem.headline: Thais capture Khmer Rouge hardliner - Cambodian PM.

text.p: Thailand has arrested a fugitive Khmer Rouge hardliner but may refuse to extradite him, Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said on Saturday.

The Cambodian government believes at least four senior Khmer Rouge hardliners, including defence chief Son Sen and Pol Pot's right-hand man, Nuon Chea, fled across the border to Thailand on the fall of their key Samlaut base late last month.
"One of them was arrested among four... There are three left and they can arrest them if they want," Ranariddh told reporters in the capital. He refused to name the guerrilla leader.
But he noted that Bangkok had refused to extradite former interior minister Sin Song, an alleged ringleader of a failed 1994 coup bid, after he escaped from custody.
"Thailand refused to send him to Cambodia and I fear will do the same for those (hardliners)," he said.

Analysts said the issue could damage bilateral relations, now warming after Phnom Penh in 1994 accused Thai businessmen and elements of the military of helping Khmer Rouge guerrillas fight the coalition government.

Ranariddh said he and Second Prime Minister Hun Sen had written to Thai Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa asking that Thailand capture and extradite the hardliners. But he added that they might have to wait until a new Thai government is formed after the November election.
Banharn last week dissolved the government and ordered general elections.
"The ball is on the Thai side...it would be simply political will and you know that the government in Thailand is a temporary one," Ranariddh said at a Transport Ministry ceremony.

Khmer Rouge guerrillas loyal to Ieng Sary, who was foreign minister during Pol Pot's genocidal 1975-79 Khmer Rouge regime, have been talking with the government about peace and a merger of their forces in the northwest.
The hardliners lost their toehold in the area with the fall of Samlaut but still control large areas in the north and have influence in the southwest.

The Khmer Rouge, which oversaw the deaths of more than one million people in the late 1970s, signed a U.N.-brokered peace pact with rivals in 1991. They reneged on the accord and have been fighting the coalition that emerged from elections in 1993.
